content: Edema refers to the abnormal accumulation of fluid in the interstitial spaces of the body. This condition arises due to various mechanisms, including increased hydrostatic pressure, decreased oncotic pressure, enhanced capillary permeability, or obstruction of lymphatic drainage. Edema can result from systemic diseases such as nephrotic syndrome, right-sided heart failure, hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism, adverse effects of certain medications, complications following recent surgeries, or malignancies. It may present as generalized edema, often associated with cardiac, thyroid, or kidney diseases, or as localized edema, which can be caused by conditions like cellulitis, deep vein thrombosis (DVT), chronic venous insufficiency, or lymphedema. The diagnostic process involves a thorough history-taking, focusing on recent surgeries, trauma, systemic illnesses, malignancies, and a physical examination to assess the distribution of edema. The examination also determines whether the edema is pitting or non-pitting and evaluates for pain upon palpation. Duplex ultrasonography is a valuable tool for identifying evidence of DVT. In cases of localized edema with an unclear cause, further imaging studies such as abdominal computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance venography may be necessary. Causes of Peripheral Edema Life-Threatening Causes: Generalized edema due to decompensated heart failure. Localized leg edema caused by proximal DVT, which can lead to acute pulmonary embolism. Common Causes: Advanced kidney disease. Nephrotic syndrome. Systolic or diastolic heart failure. Constrictive pericarditis. Pulmonary hypertension. Anemia. Nutritional deficiencies or malabsorption. Refeeding edema. Deep vein thrombosis. Cellulitis. Superficial thrombophlebitis. Baker’s cyst. Chronic venous insufficiency. Lymphedema. Pregnancy. Menstrual cycle-related edema. Hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism. Medication-induced edema. Obstructive sleep apnea. Diagnosis The diagnostic approach to edema involves an algorithmic evaluation, which includes history-taking, physical examination, and appropriate imaging or laboratory studies to identify the underlying cause. Treatment The treatment of edema is guided by an algorithm that addresses the underlying cause and employs specific therapeutic interventions. Recommendations for Management: Before initiating medical compression therapy, arterial circulation should be assessed. If foot or ankle pulses are weak or absent, the ankle-brachial index (ABI) should be measured. In cases of proximal DVT, the use of compression bandages or medical compression stockings, combined with walking and anticoagulant therapy, can reduce pain and swelling. Medical compression in DVT does not increase the risk of pulmonary thromboembolism or post-thrombotic syndrome. Early mobilization in acute DVT does not elevate the risk of pulmonary thromboembolism. During the acute phase of DVT, calf compression can minimize irreversible skin changes, edema, and pain. In compensated heart failure (NYHA Class I and II), mild compression of both legs may improve cardiac preload. Proper sizing of compression therapy is crucial in diabetic neuropathy to prevent peripheral nerve damage, such as peroneal nerve palsy and foot drop. Obstructive sleep apnea in obese patients can cause bilateral leg edema due to hypoxia-induced pulmonary hypertension. After harvesting leg veins for bypass graft surgery, mild compression stockings (15–20 mmHg) significantly reduce leg edema. Daflon or micronized purified flavonoid fraction (MPFF) is recommended for chronic venous insufficiency due to its anti-inflammatory effects and enhancement of venous contractility. Topical steroids may be beneficial for stasis dermatitis (characterized by scaling and erythematous skin changes) associated with chronic venous insufficiency and lymphedema. Contraindications for Compression Therapy: Severe arterial insufficiency (e.g., ankle pressure <60 mmHg, transcutaneous oxygen pressure <20 mmHg). Suspected compression of bypassed arteries in coronary artery bypass graft surgery. Severe decompensated heart failure (NYHA Class IV) due to increased preload, which can worsen ventricular function. History of allergic reactions to compression materials. Severe diabetic neuropathy with sensory loss, microangiopathy, and risk of skin necrosis.
